profile.documented: This model is configured as a chat model with documented text, vision, tools, and structured-output capabilities, a 262144-token context limit, and multilingual coverage. Thinking mode is a toggle, so reasoning can be switched on or off per request. No model-specific adapter is documented for it.
profile.role_in_run: HOME-22 (Vision tool calling) was designed around this model. That test shows the model a form image plus a goal and requires exactly one correct tool call, which measures whether vision understanding survives the jump into function calling.

overall.rating_basis: Mean quality 0.697 across 21 scored tests, home-test quality 0.900, exact-answer rate 0.670. The rating follows the shared formula with no adjustment.

home_test.title: Vision tool calling
home_test.analysis: This is the model's best evidence that its vision and tool skills compose: 9 of 10 cases produced exactly the expected call. The single miss called ask_user instead of read_record, asking which payment to refund when the record id was already recoverable from context. That failure mode is a cautious-clarification reflex rather than blindness, since the same run reads similar forms correctly. For form-filling agents with a validation step, this is a genuinely usable result.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: The model was still writing its private reasoning when the token limit was reached, so no final answer exists.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: The final message is empty on all 31 records; the thinking trace consumed the whole budget. This hits every reasoning-heavy test (10 cases on competition math, 6 on constrained optimization, 7 on bug repair, 8 on code generation).
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Anyone using this model for math or code work must budget far more thinking tokens or the answer never arrives.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: The answer is semantically right but breaks the required output contract.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: On chart reading it returned the right value wrapped in a JSON code fence, for example answering 247 correctly but inside triple backticks the contract forbids. Lenient parsing recovers full credit, strict credit is zero.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Downstream code that parses the answer strictly will reject correct results unless a lenient fallback is added.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A structured answer got most fields right but at least one field wrong.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: On multilingual message classification the model kept intent, entities, amount, date, and language correct but graded urgency low where medium was expected, scoring 0.833 on that case.
failure_analysis.example_quote: {"intent": "delivery_change", "urgency": "low", "entity_ids": ["ORD-66035"], "amount": 63, "date": "2026-09-06", "language": "es"}
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Single-attribute slips like urgency are the typical residual error when this model otherwise understands the request.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A converted document differs from the reference in wording or markup details.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: On HTML-to-Markdown conversion it reproduces the structure (headings, lists, links all near perfect) but rewords sentences, for example writing its own guide phrasing instead of the reference text, keeping token overlap near 0.99 but never exact.

# New Engineer Onboarding

This guide explains `make setup` with a **first Friday demo** setup and an *open questions*.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Output needs a human review pass wherever exact wording matters, even though the structure is trustworthy.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A tool-loop turn violated the interaction contract even though individual calls looked plausible.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: The final message is empty and the recorded calls show the defect, for example sending the identical refund email to the same address twice in one case instead of acting once and answering.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Duplicate side effects like double emails are the most operationally risky failure in this model's tool behavior.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A support request was sent to the wrong team queue.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: It returned a keyword-triggered route (TECH with a keyword reason code) where the policy required escalation with a missing-id reason, scoring zero on those cases.
failure_analysis.example_quote: {"route":"TECH","reason_code":"KEYWORD_TECH"}
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Keyword reflexes override policy reading on ambiguous tickets, so escalation rules need explicit emphasis in the prompt.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A SQL query ran successfully but returned the wrong set of rows.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: The queries are well-formed joins that miss part of the expected row set, for example returning 4 of 5 expected customer names because the product filter drops one qualifying row.
failure_analysis.example_quote:
SELECT DISTINCT c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Results look plausible and need row-count checks, since the SQL itself gives no sign of the miss.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A tool loop finished with the workspace in the wrong state.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: The final message is empty and the recorded state shows the defect: the calls themselves succeed but a required change is missing, for example no confirmation email recorded where the task required one.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: State checks after each tool loop are necessary because the model can do the visible work and skip the bookkeeping step.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: The final answer itself was cut off by the token limit.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: Generated code stops mid-function, for example a run-length encoder that breaks off inside its main loop, earning only 0.125 partial credit for the one hidden test it happened to satisfy.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Long code answers need a larger output budget or they arrive incomplete and unusable.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A question-answering response gave the wrong answer or abstained incorrectly.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: It returned the literal string null as the answer value where a true JSON null with abstention was expected, a type-level slip that scores zero despite looking nearly right.
failure_analysis.example_quote: {"answer": "null", "citations": [], "abstain": true}
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: String-versus-null confusion breaks strict consumers even when the model understood that no answer exists.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A response was judged wrong with no finer sub-category recorded.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: On table OCR it transcribed 17 of 18 cells correctly but read CO2 as C02, scoring 0.944; on its home vision-tool test it asked the user which payment to refund instead of reading record REC-902.

failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Single-character OCR slips and over-cautious clarification questions are the residual errors at this model's ceiling.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A safety prompt was given the wrong safe-or-unsafe label.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: It labeled prompts requiring an unsafe verdict with category S2 as safe with no categories, missing genuine policy violations rather than over-flagging.
failure_analysis.example_quote: {"label": "safe", "categories": []}
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Misses lean toward under-flagging, which is the dangerous direction for a safety classifier.

strengths: Vision and tool use compose well: 9 of 10 vision form cases produced exactly the expected single tool call on its home test.
Long-document work is excellent, with 8 of 8 wiki QA cases correct and all 20 boxed word problems solved.
Structured single-turn output is reliable: 35 of 40 routes, 29 of 30 function calls, and 29 of 32 safety labels correct.
OCR transcription is near-perfect at 14 of 16 exact with only single-character slips in the misses.
weaknesses: Reasoning traces routinely outgrow the token budget: 31 cases across math, code, and optimization produced no answer at all.
Output-contract discipline is weak: 9 chart answers fenced in code blocks and 11 document answers with broken contracts despite correct content.
Multi-step tool loops leave the workspace wrong or repeat side effects, as in the duplicated refund email.
use_when: Vision form-submission agents where each proposed tool call passes a validation check (HOME-22).
Long-document question answering with evidence citations over large contexts (HOME-09).
Multilingual support-message classification where a lenient parser reads the JSON (HOME-01).
Boxed-format math word problems and single-turn function calling (HOME-13, HOME-24).
avoid_when: Competition math or constraint optimization under tight token budgets, where reasoning is cut off before answering (HOME-04, HOME-17).
Chart question answering behind a strict parser with no lenient fallback for fenced output (HOME-05).
Unsupervised multi-step tool workflows that send real notifications, given duplicate and missing side effects (HOME-18, HOME-21).
hardware_fit: Cold load takes about 4.0 seconds and generation runs near 96 tokens per second with the full model on the GPU, so interactive chat, vision, and tool work feel responsive. Reasoning-heavy tasks still stall because the token budget, not the hardware, is the binding constraint. This is a comfortable daily-use fit for the 8GB card.
bottom_line: The most versatile vision-capable model in this group: strong across vision tools, long documents, routing, and math word problems, held back by reasoning traces that overflow the token budget and loose output-contract discipline. Give it room to think and a lenient parser, and keep a supervisor on email-sending tool loops.

strengths: Boxed math word problems are perfect at 20 of 20, and competition math reaches 10 of 12, remarkable for the smallest model in the run.
Single-turn function calling is near-perfect at 29 of 30 with clean native calls.
Template extraction hits 10 of 12 exact, and short tool loops reach 7 of 10 fully correct.
Routing on its home test is solid at 32 of 40 with a clear, single-shape error pattern.
weaknesses: Safety labels are systematically malformed: 18 of 32 cases write decorated text like S7 Privacy instead of the bare code.
Multilingual classification rarely lands exactly (6 of 24), always losing exactly one field.
Document conversion restructures pages instead of preserving them, so no conversion is ever exact.
use_when: First-line support-ticket routing with an escalation review behind it (HOME-16).
Single-turn function calling and short tool loops with native calls (HOME-24, HOME-18).
Boxed-format math word problems and template extraction from long texts (HOME-13, HOME-12).
Quick code drafts where hidden tests verify the result (HOME-14).
avoid_when: Safety classification behind a strict label gate, where malformed labels fail most cases (HOME-08).
Faithful HTML-to-Markdown conversion, since it rewrites page structure (HOME-19).
Long-context evidence QA without citation checking, given confident wrong answers (HOME-09).
Any vision or embedding work, which it has no documented capability for.
hardware_fit: Cold load takes about 2.1 seconds and generation runs near 217 tokens per second with the full model on the GPU, the fastest generalist text model in this group. It is the obvious choice when responsiveness or throughput matters most on the 8GB card, provided the task stays within text and tools.
bottom_line: A fast, small generalist that punches above its size on math, function calling, extraction, and routing, but cannot follow strict label contracts and rewrites documents instead of converting them. Best used as a quick triage and drafting model with validators behind it.

avoid_when: Interactive use on an 8GB card, where roughly 9 tokens per second makes every task feel stalled.

hardware_fit: Cold load takes about 7.8 seconds and generation runs near 9 tokens per second with only about 63 percent of the model on the GPU, the slowest setup in this group by a wide margin. On an 8GB card this model partially spills to system memory, so every long task risks the deadline. It is a poor fit for interactive use here and only viable for patient batch work.
bottom_line: The most accurate model on the work it actually attempted, and the least practical: partial GPU offload makes it so slow that half the run never happened. Choose it for offline batch tasks where correctness outweighs waiting, never for interactive sessions on this card.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A SQL query failed to execute against the database.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: It invents plausible-looking functions and columns that do not exist, for example wrapping dates in a to_number conversion the database rejects, so a quarter of its queries die at execution.
failure_analysis.example_quote: SELECT o.id AS order_id, to_number(o.order_date, 'YYYYMMDD') AS order_date
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Every generated query must be executed before use, since failures give no partial result.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A SQL query ran successfully but returned the wrong set of rows.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: It returns plausible row sets with the wrong shape, for example grouping customers with maximum order ids and dates where the question needed something narrower, matching 10 of 12 expected values.
failure_analysis.example_quote: SELECT customers.id AS customer_id, MAX(orders.id) AS max_order_id
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Wrong-shape results look authoritative and need row-level checks against the question.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: A SQL query used syntax from a different database dialect that the local database rejects.
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: It emitted Postgres-specific syntax against the local SQLite fixtures, including an ILIKE comparison on one case and a to_char date formatter on another, both rejected at parse time.
failure_analysis.example_quote: SELECT customers.name FROM customers JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Dialect discipline is the first fix to demand: without it, queries fail before their logic is even tested.

strengths: Exact SQL on 9 of 20 questions, including multi-table joins over retail and HR schemas.
Partial credit on close misses shows real query structure rather than guessing, with row-set overlap above 0.8 on two cases.
Fast generation near 88 tokens per second with the full model on the GPU keeps iteration quick.
weaknesses: A quarter of queries fail to execute from invented functions or missing columns.
Postgres-only syntax leaks into SQLite-targeted queries, a systematic dialect-discipline gap.
Wrong-shape result sets on 4 of 20 cases mean outputs need row-level verification.
use_when: Drafting analytical SQL for review where every query is executed and checked before use (HOME-20).
Simple multi-table join questions over well-described retail or HR schemas (HOME-20).
avoid_when: Direct execution of generated SQL without running it first, given the 25 percent execution-failure rate (HOME-20).
SQLite targets without a dialect check, since Postgres syntax slips through (HOME-20).
Any non-SQL task, where it has no attempt on record.
hardware_fit: Cold load takes about 2.9 seconds and generation runs near 88 tokens per second with the full model on the GPU. It is a light, responsive SQL-drafting companion on the 8GB card with no offload concerns.
bottom_line: A specialist that writes real SQL with correct join structure half the time and fails the other half on execution, dialect, or row shape. Useful as a supervised query drafter with mandatory execution checks, and nothing beyond SQL on current evidence.
